title: Sequoiadendron giganteum
description: Species of tree native to North America
wiki_lead:
Sequoiadendron giganteum (also known as the giant sequoia, giant redwood, Sierra redwood or Wellingtonia) is a species of coniferous tree, classified in the family Cupressaceae in the subfamily Sequoioideae. Giant sequoia specimens are the largest trees on Earth. They are native to the groves on the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada mountain range of California but have been introduced, planted, and grown around the world.
The giant sequoia is listed as an endangered species by the IUCN with fewer than 80,000 remaining in its native California.
The giant sequoia grow to an average height of 50–85 m (164–279 ft) with trunk diameters ranging from 6–8 m (20–26 ft). Record trees have been measured at 94.8 m (311 ft) tall. The specimen known to have the greatest diameter at breast height is the General Grant tree at 8.8 m (29 ft). Giant sequoias are among the oldest living organisms on Earth. The oldest known giant sequoia is 3,200–3,266 years old.
Wood from mature giant sequoias is fibrous and brittle; trees would often shatter after they were felled. The wood is unsuitable for construction and instead is used for fence posts or match sticks. The giant sequoia is a very popular ornamental tree in many parts of the world.

Evolutionary history and taxonomy
A close relative to the giganteum is the Sequoia sempervirens, which lives in an area on the coast of the Pacific Coast of North America. The earliest relatives of the giganteum existed in the Cretaceous Period. The oldest fossil in the Sequoiadendron genus is from the Miocene Epoch. These existed roughly 10-20 million years ago and are likely the direct ancestor of the giganteum. The fossil belongs to a tree from the Sequoiadendron chaneyi.
About 5-10 million years ago, during the late miocene epoch, ancestors of the giganteum existed in western Nevada, but moved west as the climate became cooler and drier. This eventually led to the settling of the Sequoiadendron in the Sierra Nevada.
Today, there are only 3 living species in the subfamily Sequoioideae. Each of them are in their own genus. The first two are the Sequoiadendron giganteum and the Metasequoia glyptostroboides. The last is the Sequoia sempervirens. There has been research to show that S. sempervirens may have come into fruition as an ancient hybrid between ancestors of the giant sequoia and Metasequoia.
Within the Sequoiadendron genus, there are only 3 species, one of which, have survived to today (giganteum). One of the other species is tchucoticum. Its shoots are closest to the giganteum. They existed during the Late Cretaceous period. The tchucoticum existed in the Enmyvaam River Basin in Russia. The other species is chaneyi. This existed until the late Miocene, mostly in western Nevada.

grok_lead: Sequoiadendron giganteum, commonly known as the giant sequoia or Sierra redwood, is a long-lived coniferous tree species in the cypress family Cupressaceae, endemic to scattered groves on the western slopes of California's Sierra Nevada mountains between 1,300 and 2,400 meters elevation. These massive evergreens are distinguished by their exceptional size and age, with mature specimens routinely exceeding 50 meters in height and 7 meters in diameter at breast height, thick spongy reddish bark rich in tannins that confers fire resistance, and scale-like foliage. By stem volume, they represent the largest trees on Earth, exemplified by the General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park, which measures approximately 1,487 cubic meters. Individual trees can attain ages of over 3,000 years, with the oldest verified specimen dated to 3,266 years. Native to roughly 75 isolated groves spanning a 420-kilometer altitudinal belt, giant sequoias thrive in deep, well-drained granitic soils within mixed conifer forests, where they form codominant stands alongside species like sugar pine and white fir. Their reproduction relies on fire-scarified serotinous cones, which release seeds post-disturbance, historically maintained by frequent low-intensity wildfires that cleared competing vegetation and reduced fuels for catastrophic burns. However, century-scale fire exclusion policies have altered ecosystems, culminating in recent high-severity wildfires exacerbated by drought and climate shifts that have killed up to 20% of mature trees since 2020, prompting endangered status assessments. Widely cultivated ornamentally outside their narrow native range due to adaptability in temperate climates, giant sequoias have been planted globally, including in the United Kingdom and New Zealand, though non-native populations lack the genetic diversity and scale of wild groves. Iconic specimens like the General Grant Tree, designated the Nation's Christmas Tree, underscore their cultural significance, while ongoing restoration efforts emphasize prescribed burning to mimic natural regimes and mitigate decline.
